newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's 1996 tin output seen down 17 percent.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's 1996 tin output seen down 17 percent.

text.p: Malaysia's 1996 tin production is forecast to fall 17 percent due to weak prices and poor ore grades, making higher imports likely next year to feed growing local demand, an industry official said on Wednesday.

Tin ore production for the first three quarters of 1996 was 4,089 tonnes, and was expected to reach 5,300 tonnes for the full year, Muhamad Nor Muhamad, executive director of the Malaysian Chamber of Mines (MCM), told Reuters.
This compared with 6,402 tonnes produced last year.
A bouyant economy was fuelling demand for tin in the electronics, canning and pewter industries, but miners remained reluctant to increase output, Muhamad Nor said in an interview.
"The Kuala Lumpur Tin Market is virtually undermined now by speculation in copper on the London Metal Exchange," he said.
"If the price is bad, then the ore obtained from the ground is not that good either."
Prices on the Kuala Lumpur Tin Market averaged just above 15 ringgit ($5.95) per kilogram in the first three quarters of this year.
Muhamad Nor said he was certain that many miners who had diversified to other industries would return to tin if the metal's price reached about 18 ringgit ($7.14) per kilogram.
Consumption between January and September of this year was 4,528 tonnes and could reach 6,800 by year-end, compared with 6,350 for all of 1995, he said.

"We are already a net consumer and could, theoretically, be importing more next year," Muhamad Nor said. He added that it was difficult to forecast imports as they were subject to fluctuations in demand and prices.

In 1995, imports of tin-in-concentrates, or tin ore, totalled 34,871 tonnes while exports of refined or smelted tin reached 35,216 tonnes, records from the MCM, an officially recognised umbrella body for the country's miners, said.
Malaysia's booming electronics sector was the largest domestic consumer of smelted tin last year, using nearly 56 percent of Malaysia's tin ore output to solder components to circuit boards.
The canning industry, made up mostly by food and beverage manufacturers, was the second-largest consumer with 16 percent while pewter makers were third, using about seven percent.
Malaysia was the world's top tin producer two decades ago, providing a third of global output, with a record of 76,800 tonnes in 1972.
But the crash of the world tin market in 1985 after a glut in production ended the good times for the local tin industry, which now contributes about 2.7 percent of world output.

Muhamad Nor said that with the decline in ore grades at secondary mining sources such as rivers, producers would have to shift to primary areas such as mountain ranges to find quality tin if they seriously considered increasing production.
"This will require going deep into the ground and means more expenses," he said. "With the high labour and production cost in Malaysia, nobody in the right sense of mind would want to do this."
